title: 𓂋𓄿 𓏌𓅱 𓉐𓂋𓏏𓂻 𓅓 𓉔𓂋𓅱𓇳
titleEn: Book of the Dead of Ani — Spells 74, 8, 2, 9, 132 and 10
part: Spells 74, 8, 2, 9, 132 and 10 — walking, going forth by day, living after death and returning home (Plate 18)
work: Book of the Dead of Ani
workEn: Book of the Dead of Ani
draftNote: Draft — the hieroglyphs are read from the printed type of Budge's 1895 edition of the papyrus, and the signs and readings are still being checked; expect changes.
source: Papyrus of Ani (British Museum EA 10470), Plate XVIII. Hieroglyphs transcribed from the interlinear text of E. A. W. Budge, The Book of the Dead: The Papyrus of Ani in the British Museum (London, 1895), pp. 118–122; Budge's transliteration and word-by-word English were used to check the reading of the signs and the sense, never for wording. Only the papyrus's own text is given: the passages Budge supplies from other papyri in his appendixes and footnotes are left out. Transliteration in the Leiden convention, with the reed written i; translation made fresh from the Egyptian. Shown left to right; the papyrus is written in columns read from the top down. The line under each word ("say") is the conventional Egyptological classroom pronunciation — a neutral e between consonants; ꜣ and ꜥ as a; w as u or w; ṯ as tj; ḏ as dj; ḫ and ẖ as kh; š as sh — an artificial teaching pronunciation, since the vowels of Egyptian were never written. The grouping of signs within a word follows Budge's type, which regularises the scribe's hand.
about: Six short spells written one after another on Plate 18 of Ani's papyrus, after Spells 43, 89, 91 and 92. Spell 74 gives the dead man the use of his legs; Spells 8, 2 and 9 open the West and the world below to him so that he may go forth by day and live after death, as the Moon, as the son of Osiris and as a glorious spirit; Spell 132 lets him come back to see his house on earth; and Spell 10 (Budge's Chapter XLVIII) sends him out against his enemies. Many words are rare and several signs in Budge's print are uncertain; the notes say where a reading is doubtful, and the last spell breaks off in mid-thought.

sentences.i: Spell for hastening(?) the legs and going forth upon earth.
sentences.n: Spell 74 begins, written in red. rꜣ n 'spell of' is the mouth with its stroke and water n, as in every title. wnt is the hare wn with water n as complement, t and the walking legs as classifier: wn 'hasten, hurry', the verb of motion written with the legs (as in Spells 46 and 92), here with a t that the infinitive of a verb of two consonants does not take, so the form is not clear (an infinitive or a noun); Budge has 'walking', and the sense is doubtful. rdwy 'the two legs' is the leg with its foot (D56) printed twice, the first as the word-sign rd, the second for the dual; the ending wy is not written. No preposition stands between them: 'hastening the legs', making them move quickly. pr 'going forth' is the house pr with r and the walking legs, the infinitive of pri, its t not written. tꜣ 'earth' is the strip of land with grains (coded N16, approximate). The dead man asks for the use of his legs, so that he can walk out of the tomb.

sentences.i: Said by the Osiris Ani: May you do your deeds (for me?), Sokar (Twice.),
sentences.n: The papyrus writes i and r; read in. ḏd in N 'said by N' is written in red: the cobra with an upright stroke under its neck, the cobra-and-hand ligature of this type, coded I10 and D46 (the hand approximate), then the reed over a lens-shaped sign that is the mouth r, where water n belongs; the formula allows only in. wsir is the low seat (coded Q2, approximate) over the eye, in black. ir·k is the eye ir with r as complement and the basket ·k: the sḏm·f of iri 'do', here a wish or command, 'may you do'. irt·k is the same eye and r with t, plural strokes and ·k: the noun irt 'what is done, deeds', from iri (not irt 'eye'), 'your deeds'. Water n follows and is not clear: perhaps the preposition 'for' with its object 'me' not written, or the genitive 'your deeds of (= as) Sokar'; the translation marks it doubtful. skr 'Sokar' is the bolt s, the basket k and r with the seated god (Budge: Seker). sp sn '(Twice.)' is the threshing floor sp (O50) and two upright strokes: the call is to be said twice. Sokar is the falcon god of the Memphite cemetery, made one with Osiris; his feast was the moving of his bark, and he is asked here to do his work in the dead man.

sentences.n: ink 'I' is the pot in (W24) with k and the seated man as classifier: ink with a noun, 'I am …'. psd 'one who shines' is p, the bolt s and a low flat hand d, with the sun shedding rays (N8) as classifier: the participle of psḏ 'shine', spelled with the hand d for ḏ, as in the Hymn to Ra. ḥry 'who is over' is the face ḥr with r, two strokes y and the sky as classifier: the nisba of ḥr 'upon'. wꜥrt 'the Leg' is a single leg with its foot (D56), the word-sign, with t as complement (Budge: uart); wꜥrt pt, 'the Leg of the Sky', is a direct genitive, and pt 'sky' is p and t with the sky sign. sentences.n: pr·i 'I come forth' is the house pr with r, the walking legs and the seated man ·i: the sḏm·f of pri. m pt 'from the sky' as before. ḥfd·i is the wick ḥ, the viper f and the hand d, with a man seated as if on a chair with one arm raised (coded A50, approximate) as classifier and ·i (Budge: ḥefṭ-à): a verb ḥfd, taken by its classifier as 'sit, settle'; the sense is doubtful. ḥr 'at, beside' is the face with its stroke. ꜣḫw is the crested ibis ꜣḫ (G25) and the chick w, with the sun with rays and the seated god as classifiers (Budge's numeral 3 is printed inside the word): ꜣḫ 'spirit'. sentences.n: m ḥr 'in the face of, before' is the owl m and the face with its stroke and r (Budge's numeral 4 is printed before the r). ibḥw 'the teeth' is a small tusk (coded F18, approximate), the sign of the tooth, over plural strokes (Budge: ābeḥ, with the arm ꜥ, which is not printed either); the word is taken as ibḥ 'tooth', its reed i not printed. ṯꜣ is a duckling with raised wings (coded G47, approximate), the sign ṯꜣ, with the vulture ꜣ as complement: taken as ṯꜣ 'seize, snatch', a participle 'that seize' (Budge: t'a, that is ḏꜣ, 'gnasheth'; the duckling is the sign of ṯꜣ, and no ḏ is printed). After tp Budge prints four dots in his transliteration, but no gap in the signs; the kneeling man, which does not usually follow tp, may be what he could not read, and the sense 'head' is doubtful. ḏḥwty 'Thoth' is the ibis on its standard with t and two strokes y. Wenu, Thoth's city, is where the world was said to begin; the opening and sealing are perhaps of his shrine.

sentences.i: Excellent is the Eye of Horus, which binds(?) me; the glorious Eye of Horus is my ornament(s) on the brow of Ra, the father of the gods.
sentences.n: iqr 'excellent' is the reed, the hill-slope q, r and a flat roll (Y1) as classifier: an adjective put first as the predicate, 'excellent is …'. irt ḥr 'the Eye of Horus' is the plain eye with t and its stroke, and the falcon with a stroke (Budge: maat, another word for the eye; the t and stroke after the plain eye give irt). Budge prints seśeṭu-à as one group; it is split here into sšd and wi (q re-indexed), as in the same words in Spell 92: sšd is a looped cord (coded V6, approximate) for sš and the low flat hand d, a participle after its noun, 'which binds(?)' (Budge: 'I have delivered'), the sense doubtful; wi 'me' is the chick w and the kneeling man, the dependent pronoun. irt ḥr again, the falcon alone. ꜣḫ 'glorious' is the crested ibis, ḫ and the roll: an adjective after its noun. ḫkrw is the belly of an animal (coded F32, approximate) written for ḫ, the basket k and r, an ornament of the frieze ḫkr (coded Aa30, approximate), the roll and a stroke (Budge: χakeru, 'splendours'). After it stands the kneeling man alone, under which Budge prints only dots; it is taken here as the suffix ·i 'my', as in Spell 92 (ḫkrw·i, with a stroke and the seated man), and joined to the word (q re-indexed). The sentence has no verb: 'the glorious Eye of Horus (is) my ornaments'. m wpt rꜥ 'on the brow of Ra': the bar m, the horns wp (coded F13, approximate) with t and a stroke, and rꜥ with r, a flat arm ꜥ (coded D36, approximate) and the seated god with the sun disc. Budge's numeral 3 stands before itf 'father', the reed, t and the viper f with a seated figure (coded A1, approximate: the type shows a long-wigged figure). nṯrw 'the gods' is the flag three times. The Eye of Horus is the uraeus on the sun's brow; the dead man wears it as his own crown.

sentences.n: ḏd in is in red; wsir (the low seat, coded Q2, approximate, over the eye) is black. Ani's classifier, the kneeling man, is in Budge's square brackets, restored. i 'O' is the reed with a standing man raising an arm (coded A26, approximate). wꜥ 'One' is the harpoon wꜥ (T21) with a stroke and a low flat sign with an upright tab (coded U15 for what is printed) standing for the arm ꜥ as complement (Budge reads ā): 'the One, the Unique'. wbn 'who rises' is the chick w and the foot b, with a disc with hanging rays (coded N8, approximate) as classifier; its n is not written: the participle of wbn 'rise, shine forth'. m 'as' (Budge: 'from'). iꜥḥ 'the Moon' is the seated moon god with crescent and disc (coded A40, approximate), written alone. The One who rises as the Moon is the god who shines in the night sky, perhaps Thoth or Osiris.

sentences.l: let-come-forth · the-Osiris · Ani · this · among · multitude-your · that · (which-is)-outside
sentences.i: Let this Osiris Ani come forth among that multitude of yours which is outside.
sentences.n: The papyrus writes the eye ir at the head of rwty; read rwty. prt is written as in the title, house, r, t and the walking legs: with the noun after it, it is taken as a wish, 'let (him) come forth', the t not explained. wsir with the low seat (coded Q2, approximate); ꜣny with the kneeling man; pn 'this' is p and n. m 'among' is the bar m (Aa15). ꜥšꜣt·k 'your multitude' is the lizard ꜥšꜣ (I1) over plural strokes, t and ·k. twy 'that' is t, the chick w and two reeds y, the feminine demonstrative agreeing with ꜥšꜣt. The last word is the eye ir and r, the chick w, t, two strokes y and a house sign (O1), with Budge's numeral 3 printed after the eye and r; Budge's footnote (left out) corrects the eye to a second mouth r, which gives rwty 'outside, the outer (place)', the nisba of rwt 'gate, outside', with the house as classifier. 'Those outside' are the living, or the gods of the open sky, among whom the dead man would walk.

sentences.l: establish(?) · him · being-in(?) · among · the-spirits · is-opened · to-him · the-Duat
sentences.i: Establish(?) him among the spirits; the Duat is opened to him.
sentences.n: The first word is doubtful. Its first sign is a hatched, domed shape with crossed lines like a tail at its left, lying on a base line, which has no good code and is coded K1 (a fish) although the shape is not that sign; then a low flat sign with an upright tab (U15), the coil w (Z7) and the same flat sign with its left end curled up (U15). Budge reads uāu, 'let be established'. It is read here wꜥw by Budge's letters, the first sign taking his u only because he reads it so, the first U15 standing for the arm ꜥ as in wꜥ above and the second as classifier; no word wꜥw of that sense is known to this edition, and both reading and sense are guesses. sw 'him' is the sedge sw (M23) with the chick w: the dependent pronoun, the object. imyw is the crossed planks im, the coil w and two strokes: the plural nisba 'who are in', which here doubles the m that follows, 'among'. ꜣḫw 'the spirits' is written with the sun with hanging rays (coded N8, approximate) as a word-sign for ꜣḫ, the chick w, and a seated figure (coded A40, approximate) as classifier (Budge: χu, 'shining ones'): the dead who have become shining spirits. Budge prints unu-nef as one group; it is split here into wn·w and n·f (q re-indexed). wn·w is the hare, n, the chick w and a hatched door-bolt (O31) over the low hooked sign (U15) as classifiers: the passive 'is opened', as in Spell 8. n·f 'to him' is water n and ·f. dwꜣt 'the Duat' is the star, the vulture ꜣ, t and an open-bottomed house sign (Budge: Ṭuat). The Duat, the world below through which the sun passes by night, is opened before him.

sentences.l: now · the-Osiris · (Osiris) · Ani · (is)-going-forth · by · day · to · do · will-his · upon · earth · among · the-living
sentences.i: Now the Osiris Ani is going forth by day, to do what he wishes upon earth among the living.
sentences.n: The papyrus writes wsir twice; read it once. isk 'now' is the reed, a folded cloth s (S29) and the basket k: the particle that opens a statement. wsir is written first with the low seat (coded Q2, approximate) over the eye, then again, after Budge's numeral 4, with the eye, the tall seat and the seated god; Budge prints '(sic)' after the second. ꜣny with the kneeling man. prt is the house, r, t and the legs: the infinitive after its subject, with the preposition ḥr of 'is doing' not written, 'is going forth'. m hrw 'by day', hrw with the house plan h, r and the sun. r irt 'to do' is r with the infinitive of iri, the eye and t. mrt·f 'his will, what he wishes' is the hoe mr (U6) with r and t, the man with hand to mouth (A2) as classifier, and ·f: the relative form of mri 'love, wish'. tp tꜣ 'upon earth': tp is the head with its stroke, tꜣ the strip of land (coded N16, approximate). m-m 'among' is the owl twice, the second joined to the flat arm. ꜥnḫw 'the living' is ꜥnḫ with n and ḫ, the chick w, the kneeling man and a thin dashed stroke. Spell 2 ends here: the dead man goes out to live among the living.

sentences.i: Spell for going forth by day after traversing(?) the Imhet.
sentences.n: Spell 9 begins; the title is written in red. rꜣ is the mouth and its stroke, with no n after it. prt is the house, r and t, without the walking legs. hrw is the sun and its stroke. m-ḫt 'after' as in Spell 2. ꜥbꜣ is the sceptre (coded S42, approximate: an upright with a ring on top, a block, a pendant strand and a crossed ring at its foot), the foot b, the jabiru bꜣ, the vulture ꜣ and a tall upright with a tie as classifier: the word of the title of Spell 8, taken as 'traversing' (Budge: āba, 'having traversed'), its sense doubtful. imḥt is the reed, an owl m drawn without head or ears (coded G17, approximate), the bar m (the m written twice, as in Budge's àmmeḥet, and read once), the wick ḥ, t and an open-bottomed house sign (Budge: àmmeḥet, 'the tomb'): the Imhet, a region of the world below, a cavern or tomb-shaft through which the dead pass. The title promises that the dead man will come out into the day once he has passed through it.

sentences.n: ḏd in is in red. No wsir is written before ꜣny, and Ani's name has no classifier; Budge's '[Osiris]' is in his English only. i 'O' is the reed and a standing man raising an arm (coded A26, approximate). bꜣ 'Ba' is the jabiru bꜣ with the small bowl (R7) printed at its foot and not read, and a small stroke. ꜥꜣ 'great' is the lozenge-tipped column (coded O29, approximate) and a flat roll (Y1). šfyt 'awe, dignity' is a ram's head (F7), the word-sign, standing on a flat bar coded as the pool š (N37, approximate) and t: ꜥꜣ šfyt, 'great of awe', an adjective with a noun after it. sentences.i: See, I have come; I see you, I traverse(?) the Duat, I see his(?) father Osiris.
sentences.n: mk is the owl m joined to the arm ꜥ (not read) and the basket k: the particle 'see, behold'. After it the kneeling man stands alone for wi 'me', the dependent pronoun, here written without its w; Budge's māk-à is one group, kept as one word mk-wi. ii·kwi 'I have come' is the reed with legs (M18) ii, the reed and two strokes as complements, the walking legs, and the stative ending ·kwi, k, w and the seated man. Budge prints maa-à-tu as one group; it is split here into mꜣꜣ·i and tw (q re-indexed): mꜣꜣ·i is the eye with the sickle mꜣ over it, two vultures and ·i, the sḏm·f 'I see'; tw 'you' is t and the chick, the dependent pronoun. ꜥbꜣ·i is the sceptre (coded S42, approximate), b, the jabiru and the roll, with ·i: the verb of the title, 'I traverse(?)'. dwꜣt 'the Duat'. mꜣꜣ·i again, with a thin dashed stroke after it before Budge's numeral 3. itf·f is the reed, t and f, then a second viper and a seated figure: 'his father' as it stands (Budge: àtef-f, '[my] father'). The ·f has no one to refer to, and 'my father' is likely, as in the next lines, but both readings are possible and the papyrus is translated as it stands. In line 4 the same doubled viper stands in itf·i, where it cannot be ·f. wsir with the low seat (coded Q2, approximate).

sentences.l: (iw) · is-given · to-me · this · to · endure · in · the-Osiris · Ani · this · without(?) · in(?) · appearings-his …
sentences.i: There is given to me this (spell), to endure in this Osiris Ani, without(?) … in(?) his appearings …
sentences.n: iw opens the statement. Budge prints erṭā-n[à] as one group; it is split here into rdi and n·i (q re-indexed). rdi is the mouth r and a flat arm (D36): the passive sḏm of rdi 'give', 'is given'. n·i 'to me' is water n and the seated man, which Budge prints in square brackets, restored. nn 'this' is two rush plants and two water lines: the demonstrative, standing alone as a noun, here taken as the thing given, perhaps the spell itself (Budge: 'that which'). r mn 'to endure': r and mn, the game board (Y5) with n and a flat roll, the infinitive of mn 'be firm, endure' (Budge: men, '[is] everlasting'). m wsir ꜣny pn 'in this Osiris Ani': wsir with the low seat (coded Q2, approximate), and ꜣny, whose kneeling man Budge prints in square brackets, restored. The last words are not clear. The first is the placenta ḫ over a flat bar hooked down at both ends (coded U31, approximate; its value is not clear), t, three water lines, and the arms of negation (D35) as classifier, which belongs to ḫm 'not know, be ignorant of' (Budge: χemt, 'without'); it is read ḫmt by its signs, the three water lines (mw) standing for m, and the t is not explained. m is the bar m. ḫꜥw·f is a hill with rays ḫꜥ (coded N28, approximate) with a flat arm ꜥ (coded D36, approximate), the coil w, a flat roll and ·f: ḫꜥw 'appearings, crowns', from ḫꜥ 'appear in glory' (Budge gives no English for it). Budge's English breaks off here with 'without his' and a row of dots, and Spell 10 ends on the papyrus in mid-thought; what stands is translated, and the sense of the end is doubtful.
